I feel that if the story added [spoiler] one or two [/spoiler] days and provided [spoiler] a few additional cases that are both unrelated and related to the main story [/spoiler], it would greatly enhance this near-perfect game and justify the price point.

Given the current length of the story, I would not recommend buying the game at full price. If the game is on sale, then I would consider purchasing it, provided you understand that you will complete the story in 3 to 4 hours and that you likely will not play it a second time, as the story follows a fixed, very short path.

review_text_raw:
I would prefer to give this game a 5/10, but unfortunately, that's not possible on Steam, so I’m rating it negatively for interested buyers to see.

I bought the game to unravel mysteries as an FBI operative—a game I could play for several hours. The gameplay mechanics are exactly what I was hoping for, but unfortunately, some of them are only used once throughout the entire game.
The story is extremely short, with a plot that becomes obvious within the first 40 minutes of gameplay. Seriously, 2 hours of gameplay for 14€? Not to meantion an "Original Soundtrack" for another 10€. If players could skip some dialogues and cutscenes, the game would only last 30 minutes. The story feels more like a detective TV show where everything is "weird," "doesn't make sense," and "everything is interconnected."

In summary:
+ The game mechanics are awesome! - Unfortunately, their potential is wasted on a simplistic story with a soap-opera-like plot seen more than thousands of times on TV.
+ The soundtrack (not bought), sound effects, and voice acting are excellent.
- The story is simple and feels rather sloppy (95% of the ideas went into coding and mechanics, 5% into the story). Perhaps it's due to the potential for a speedrunning community?
- When I calculate the "price per hour" of the main story, this game is undoubtedly the worst in my entire game library (7€ per hour (almost 12€ if you buy the "original soundtrack"), including cutscenes and dialogues).
- The game has unskippable cutscenes (returning home), dialogues (the tutorial), and end credits, likely so that you can’t get a refund within the 2-hour Steam policy.
? If the sequel to this game will also be only 2 hours long, the developers might as well not even bother. It’s not worth the money.

If the game was a bit longer (at least 4 hours of a decent story), I would recommend it, but unfortunately, I can't.
Definitely buy it during a sale, just not now.

review_text_raw:
I really enjoyed the style of investigation and the way the story was unfolding piece by piece. However, the ending fell flat and painted my overall opinion as negative. None of your actions mattered in any shape or form, there is really only one ending to be had. The choices are just an illusion, all paths lead to the same end. I guess some people like it, but for me this immediately detached all the emotion I had invested to the game and the characters and it felt like I had waisted all that time trying to choose the right path. 

A lot of strings were also left loose, and while it may have been to tease a sequel, it did not feel satisfying. A good game should be it's own complete piece that can enjoyed without digging through a Discord server for additional info or waiting for a sequel to explain everything. 

Another grievance I have with the game lies in the save system; you can't manually save and it only happens automatically at certain checkpoints. This feels extremely outdated and forces you to either play for an unknown amount of time until you hit a checkpoint, or you have to keep starting the day over because your progress isn't saved. Just give people the option to save manually and reload from a checkpoint if they have forgotten what happened. I had to take a 10 month break from the game because the save system made playing feel like a chore - you can't just play for a few minutes (or however long you feel like playing) at a time because your progress could be all for nothing.

I think the game and the developer have a lot of potential and I believe that if the second game fixes all these issues, it can be GREAT.

review_text_raw:
The Operator is a very short (3 to 4 hours at best) interactive visual novel with good production value. The interface looks clean and easy to use, the voice acting is good, and the interactive elements are pretty decent. For a visual novel. 

It is presented, however, as a game of deduction and puzzle solving. The puzzles and deductions are shallow with too much handholding. As you progress new mechanics are introduced, and then discarded immediately after. This gives the mistaken impression that much more content is waiting for you and puzzles will get more difficult. And then the game is over.

The story is equally shallow. The opening scene reveals too much, making the big reveal at the end something you can piece together within a few minutes of playing the game. The ending is a cliffhanger of sorts, but it makes this game feel like the opening chapter of a larger story that has not been written. Worse is that none of the conspiracy is ever explained, leaving you with many questions that are unlikely to be answered. There are no divergent paths, only one ending, and zero replay value.

If you go into this game expecting a visual novel, you will have an entertaining few hours with an okay story and underwhelming finale. If you go into this game expecting deduction, investigation, and puzzle solving, you will find only disappointment. This ultimately leads to my negative review. For a visual novel it is too short with an unresolved story, and for an investigation game the puzzles are too simple. The Operator has a lot of unmet potential, which is a shame.

review_text_raw:
This game only has one ending, and only less than 2½ - 3 hours of content in total, making the cost per played hour very high. 
The one singular ending is quite bad, and even though there are many dialogue options, there are no actual meaningful choices to be made.
There are numerous quite long and somewhat boring unskippable cut scenes. However one could argue that having no skip option is acceptable due to it being somewhat important to pay attention to the them. And since there's only one ending, there's no replayability, and so there's no need to have a skip option. Though realistically, and as others have pointed out, the most probable reason for not having a skip option is to extend the required playtime to over 2 hours so the game cannot be refunded through Steam.
The game has a lot of dialogue, and not a lot of gameplay. What little actual gameplay there is, is enjoyable enough I guess, but also pretty simplistic and easy. This can be seen as both a positive and a negative. If you're looking for any sort of a challenge/puzzle, you will not find it in this game. This game should be definitely thought of as a visual novel more than a puzzle game.
The story itself is mediocre and actually pretty shallow, which is very bad for a game that consists mainly of the story.
The dialogue is fully voice-acted (except for [spoiler]HAL[/spoiler] and the protagonist), which is a definite plus. The voice acting is also pretty high-quality. However I cannot help but feel like way too much developer effort and money was put into the voice acting, when it should've been put into other aspects of the game.
The soundscape and the soundtrack are also good, but really nothing out of the ordinary.

Overall, The Operator is a short, pricey mediocre dialogue-heavy and minimal-gameplay game with high-quality voice acting and heavy hand-holding and railroading, and with only one ending. It feels like the game was designed to be just long enough to make it impossible to refund after reaching the ending (which in fairness one shouldn't do regardless, if they enjoyed the game and reached the ending).

I cannot recommend anything else but to watch someone else such as a YouTuber play this game. I think that will actually add way more to the experience than buying the game and playing it on your own.

review_text_raw: The concept of the operator is super interesting. But unfortunately there's not a lot to explore and investigate here. We're constantly guided by other characters and told the very thing we need to find, one thing after the next. It's like the game never gets past the tutorial, and it never gets to the point where you get to do more advanced research. This simple game mechanic is not super satisfying. It feels more like a short story turned into a game than a real detective game. It's on a very different level compared to other detective games such as Return of the Obra Dinn, The Roottrees are Dead or The Case of the Golden Idol. It's also very short, I finished it in less than 4 hours and there's no replayability. Also be very careful with the saves, there are save points and you'll lose progress if you don't quit at exactly the right times. On the plus side, the interface is quite well done and the voices are nice (though I'm not sure why it makes my computer boiling hot when the graphics are so simple). I liked the bomb defusing part the most, and it's a shame we can't replay that part again.

The Operator is a 5/10 for me. I just didn’t like it, and the ending honestly pissed me off. It felt dumb. I went into this game thinking I’d be connecting the dots, using my brain, cracking a case, or at least acting like the man in the chair. I expected some detective-style depth, and yeah, I knew there’d be a story, but not this kind of story.

Gameplay & Expectations
I watched the trailer, played the demo, and at first I was excited. The gameplay itself was fun for what it was, and I thought it would build into something bigger. Instead, it just… ended. The ending was surprising, sure, but it wasn’t good. It left me feeling like all that build-up led nowhere.

Replay Value
There’s barely any replay value. No unlimited mode, no side content, nothing to keep you going after finishing the story. And if I remember correctly, there’s not much you can do to actually change the ending, so I had zero motivation to replay it.

Final Thoughts
It’s a fun little game on sale, but I’d recommend watching a video and playing the demo before you consider buying it. Once I beat it, I felt completely done with

kinda wish i could leave a "mixed" review because i don't hate this game - it does a lot of cool and interesting things and scratches a little bit at an itch left by hypnospace outlaw and home safety hotline, however the game is extremely short (a casual run through is about 3 hours, i can imagine someone who understands and quickly solves all the puzzles immediately on their first playthrough could potentially complete it in half that time,) the game introduces multiple puzzle mechanics that it uses exactly once and never returns to, and it has zero replayability - there is only one ending, the nature of which i imagine many will find unsatisfying due to the negative outcome for the player character and his allies. this is in spite of the player SEEMINGLY having some control over the events that take place, but ultimately have no impact on the end of the game. the feeling i got by the end of the post-credits sequence was that i had just paid 16 bucks for just the prologue to the "real game" which doesn't exist.

review_text_raw:
This review is unfortunate, because as much as I'd like to recommend the game, there's a few gripes I have with it.

First and foremost, I want to stress, this game is great and has a good hook for its plot. The mechanics it employs are varied and fun, and you do get to feel like an FBI agent working on cases alongside others. The game does a lot to nail the feel and vibe, the UI is also great and intuitive. The game's main issue isn't one singular thing, rather, it's a collection of small, minor nitpicks that ultimately end up souring the entire experience. Without trying to spoil anything, I'm going to try and summarise my complaints. 

First and foremost, the ending left me wanting. If there was an alternate ending you could achieve by using information you've gathered, it'd be one thing, but you don't get to do anything and then it just sort of ends abruptly, teasing a sequel or DLC. This is the very definition of a cliffhanger, and as such, extremely unsatisfying.

This could have been remedied if the game length was longer. But the game's barely clocking in 3 hours, you could probably beat it in 2. And, likely because of said short runtime, the game features a very small cast of characters. This unfortunately results in a somewhat predictable list of potential suspects, lessening any impacts felt from reveals that you likely saw coming.

Perhaps my biggest disappointment with how short the game was, is that the actual mechanics were unique and interesting! The puzzles were good and it introduced so many systems, one time you're analyzing chemical compounds based on formulas, another time you're disarming a bomb while given a huge manual of possibilities. And each of these varied activities happens exactly once. You spend all that time learning, understanding and mastering a skill only for it to literally not be relevant again.

This all could have perhaps been remedied by a sort of "endless mode" that generates cases and solutions, but that does not exist. And likely never will, because the game is far more focused on "immersion" as a central mechanic than gameplay. You spend a good solid 20 minutes of said 3 hours being forced to watch "immersive" unskippable cutscenes that did not need to last as long as they did. I say "immersive", because they use minimalism and only show you blurry, obfuscated imagery, which is kind of neat and saves on budget, but also means you don't even get eye candy.

Ultimately, this feels like a passion project with the wrong focus, which is a shame, because what it does right, it excels at. It's difficult to recommend this when there's games such as Cyber Manhunt 1 & 2 out that cost less and are far, far more superior in terms of value and vision. The devs are talented, and I will keep a close eye on any of their future projects, but if "The Operator 2" doesn't provide something substantially more... substantial, I can't see myself recommending that either.

review_text_raw:
I can't really recommend this game for the price being asked.

The Operator has a lot of good things going for it, the premise and story are interesting and the puzzle gameplay keeps itself fresh so nothing feels tedious. Special mention must be made about the high quality of the sound design - both the voice acting and the choice and timing of the music stings are excellent.

The biggest problem with The Operator for me is that it all falls apart just as it was gaining momentum. The last set of puzzles lack the sense of discovery from earlier, the game abruptly ends leaving a bunch of unanswered questions, and you're left feeling like nothing you did mattered.

This feels like the kind of game that should have multiple endings or changes caused by the player decisions, but there is nothing like that here. This is a specific story that you're being taken on a ride for - one with a pretty obvious "twist" - and no replayability.

If this was a prologue or chapter one of a larger game I would feel more favourable to this, but in its current state I wouldn't recommend this unless it's at least half price.

Overall, The Operator is a bland and forgettable experience. It lacks depth, variety, and replay value, making it hard to recommend.

TLDR - would not buy. knowing this is a movie you just nudge along.
Linear game, where choices don't matter at all. Interesting story-line, and puzzles you'll only solve once, but not enough to justify paying even half price for the game (from an enjoyment/replay value perspective). It's a one and done, no replay value whatsoever. Better off watching a play-through on YouTube.

PROS, but:
All elements of the game could be built towards a randomized investigative type game (look at "Papers, please" or the game described below and then apply the principles to this type of game play).  
Bomb-defusal mini-game was innovative and tense, could have multiple scenarios play out.

A similar type of game that accomplished this was Sid Meier's Covert Operations. If the type of game-play "The Operator" presents is what you're looking for and you can stomach very retro gaming (this was an DOS era game), would recommend checking out Covert Operations instead.

But again, the story is compelling. Will look to see if the sequel's gaming experience expands in a way I was hoping this game would play out: not as a movie, but a game where the player has actual agency in the world.

To the Devs:
You have a lot of components in hand to assemble a compelling, unique "radiant" type investigative game with an engaging story (or stories) lying beneath the surface to draw the player into the game's world. Looking forward with cautious optimism to see how the sequel(s) plays out.

To simplify (somewhat) integrating multiple endings (and this doesn't have to be visible to the players, or could be some sort of end of day report/summary), continue with the the day to day system, and use the day end to grade the player's actions and, using key flagged actions (as a suggestion: timing when completed could affect endings too - in time, late, way too late, done wrong, etc), lead them towards whatever multiple endings are created in the next (probably third) game.

review_text_raw:
While a very polished and well-crafted experience, this game has a number of fatal flaws that undermine and eventually irrevocably cripple your enjoyment of it.  Firstly, it's incredibly short.  I do understand that this tends to be the case for these kinds of games, crafting content for them is much more effort intensive than it is for other genres, but even by the standards of other games in this genre, you get very little playtime compared to its cost.  This is further exacerbated by a complete lack of replay value, as the story is completely linear and has no alternate endings, though there are a few pieces of content not central to the story that the player can find through their own initiative.  If you take nothing else from this review and do decide to buy the game, buy it on sale, the existing content doesn't really justify the price point.

To get into the real reasons this is a negative review, as money alone wouldn't have been enough to get me to write this, we need to first revisit the game's linearity.  The game does provide the illusion of choice, but none of the choices the player can make matter, and acting as though they do will inevitably see the game yanking on your leash and railroading you back to the single story it wants to tell.  This linearity continues to the mysteries that form the game's content, as they are designed so that the player is forced to solve them linearly as well.  Rather than providing multiple angles of attack, players must solve one specific part of a mystery before progressing to the next one, so for the most part you don't get that feeling of everything coming together as multiple clues and leads snap together into a single image, though there are exceptions to this.  I can't get too much into the ending without spoiling players, but it was abrupt, unsatisfying, and served to terminate any remaining sense of agency I had.  Everything I had accomplished was undone in an instant, in a way that felt, frankly, disrespectful and contemptuous to me as a player.  The entire point of a game, the thing that fully differentiates it from other forms of media, is that the person consuming it has agency, is not simply a passive observer but actively engages with and shapes the piece of media that they are consuming.  Of all the games I've played, this embraces that principle the least, and suffers for it.

The ultimate sin of The Operator, however, the one no detective game can be forgiven for, is its predictability.  I am in no way talented when it comes to mysteries.  When I play a detective game, read a mystery novel, or watch a movie in those genres, I am generally unable to put together the pieces ahead of time and figure out the twist before it is presented to me.  This was not the case with The Operator.  I was able to determine most of the major narrative twists well ahead of time, because they were fairly obviously telegraphed.  There were a few that were well done, and there were some that would have been very good if other obvious elements hadn't telegraphed them ahead of time.  Anyone playing this game will likely figure out its main narrative twists well before they are presented to the player, and that is truly tragic.

Anyone playing this game will likely figure out its main narrative twists well before they are presented to the player, and that is truly tragic.
